 BUSSW Institute & Partners Release Data Showing Thousands of Children Could Lose Tax Credits Under Proposed Rule
 Picture a family where a parent works full time, files taxes every year, and is raising a child who is a U.S. citizen. Today, that family may qualify for two of the nation’s most effective anti-poverty programs. Under a rule proposed this past summer, they might not.
 That is the concern behind new estimates released by the Research to Action Hub for Children in Immigrant Families, a collaboration launched by the Institute for Equity in Child Opportunity & Healthy Development (IECOHD) at Boston University School of Social Work, the Center on Poverty and Social Policy at Columbia University, and the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy.
 What the Proposed Tax Rule Would Change
 On Aug. 20, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service proposed limiting who can claim the refundable portion of four tax credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit. Only immigrants in certain legal categories would keep access.
 Because eligibility would hinge on the status of the person filing the return, a parent’s status could cost a family its refund even when every child is a U.S. citizen. Those most likely to be affected hold Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals protection, Temporary Protected Status, or temporary work and student visas.
 Treasury projects the rule would reach 200,000 to 700,000 taxpayers. The Hub’s analysis counts every member of an affected household, and the total is considerably larger.
 New Estimates Show Significant Impact on Children in Immigrant Families
 Looking at the two largest credits, the Hub’s policy brief estimates that:
 About 602,000 people, including 279,000 children, could lose the Earned Income Tax Credit.
 About 1.03 million people, including 523,000 children, could lose the refundable part of the Child Tax Credit.
 About 515,000 people, including 258,000 children, could lose both.
 Because many families would lose both credits, the groups overlap and should not be added together. Roughly 9 in 10 of the affected children are U.S. citizens.
 The stakes are high. In 2025, these two credits moved 6.1 million people, including 3.3 million children, out of poverty. Treasury reports that people claiming at least one of the four affected credits will receive an average refund of $3,656 this year.
 Why the Research to Action Hub Matters
 Federal data rarely show where children stand based on their family’s immigration status, which has left research on this group in pieces. The Hub was formed to bring that evidence together and to estimate what policy changes mean for these children. The work reflects IECOHD’s focus on equitable social policy, particularly access for immigrant families.
 The estimates rest on 2023 Census Bureau survey data and a model that infers immigration status. They may change as immigration policy and court rulings evolve. More Hub releases are planned in the coming months.
 Tax Refunds are Vital for Many Families
 For families living close to the margin, a tax refund can decide whether the month ends in balance. As the proposed rule moves forward, the Hub’s work puts a number on what is at stake for families and their children who are, overwhelmingly, American citizens.
